title: Shooting inquest jury has no recommendations
subtitle: Shot Burlington man had history of mental illness; believed police tracked him by satellite
article: An inquest jury's verdict in the 2011 police shooting death of Carl Kim makes no recommendations to prevent similar deaths.

The jury, which returned their verdict Thursday, said Kim's death was a "homicide." The categorization carries no legal or criminal judgment and simply means Kim died as a result of the actions of another person and not through lack of oversight, accident or natural causes.

That other person was Halton Regional Police Constable Michael Cairns, who shot and killed Kim at the end of a violent, 90-second struggle which followed a traffic stop on Walkers Line in Burlington on March 12, 2011. Portions of that struggle were caught on a passerby's cellphone video and a 911 exchange and were played for the inquest jury.

The jury's choice not to make any recommendations for procedural or policy changes was in keeping with the urgings of police and the coroner, who both said this shooting of a man in mental distress was a unique circumstance and no recommendations the jury could make would be able to prevent similar deaths.
Kim's family was not present for the two-day inquest, nor were they represented by a lawyer.

Coroner's counsel Kelli Frew said Kim's parents were invited, but declined to participate in the inquest, and noted the family was "deeply ashamed" of their son's illness and that it necessitated turning to the police for help.

The jury heard very little about Kim during the inquest, aside from descriptions of his wildly oscillating actions during three encounters with Halton police, the first in 2009 and two on the day he died in 2011.
What they did hear painted a picture of a volatile, delusional man subject to instant, wild rages. He was also a kick-boxer who didn't believe in medication.
Mental health worker Peggy Coughlin-Smith testified Kim's rages appeared to have "two significant triggers: his parents and police."
"He believed his parents betrayed him and he believed the police were tracking him through the water mains, trying to recruit him for a 'Fight Club.'"
Kim also believed police tracked him in his car via satellite.

No medical evidence - aside from Kim's autopsy report - was presented to the jury. And although reference was made to a number of contacts with police and Halton's Crisis Outreach and Support Team (COAST - which Coughlin-Smith is part of), no police records were detailed or presented in evidence.
But the narrative evidence the jury did hear about Kim was at times chilling.
Coughlin-Smith testified she saw Kim's abrupt change in demeanour during a 2009 police visit sparked by Kim's parents, who were said to be fearful for their lives.

During the 2009 episode, Kim's father locked himself in his bedroom for protection and called police, telling them Kim had hit him in the head, torn a phone from the wall, punched a hole in another wall and stabbed the family fridge with a kitchen knife, Coughlin-Smith testified.

Kim opened the door to police, let them in, and initially appeared quite controlled - if unhappy - Coughlin-Smith said. However, when his mother appeared Kim "burst towards her," angry and yelling. He had to be removed and restrained by tactical squad members who'd accompanied Coughlin-Smith to the home.
Other episodes stretched back to 2008, the jury was told, and included police visits and hospitalizations.
An investigation by the province's Special Investigations Unit determined Cairns was justified in using lethal force against Kim.
Presiding coroner Dr. James Kovacs thanked the jury for their service Thursday, noting that they'd been attentive, diligent and had "asked lots of very intelligent questions."
